fact_check_log.claim: Mykonos sits in the heart of the Cyclades and is known as the island of the winds.
Its name has long been shorthand for cosmopolitan, luxury holidays.
The picture couples carry with them is a real one: paved lanes, white houses, small chapels, dry-stone walls and the windmills that serve as the island's trademark.
In Hora, the main town, the Little Venice neighbourhood has houses built right against the sea.
Hora and Little Venice** suit couples who want guests close to the life of the town, with houses built against the sea and the windmills above.
The beaches** suit couples who picture a ceremony with the sand below and dinner by a pool. Mykonos Blu offers wedding experiences on Psarou beach with the sunset as a backdrop.
Royal Myconian lists a private spot on Elia Beach among its event settings.
Ftelia Bay Hotel sits on Ftelia Beach.
The sunset coast** suits couples who want the light to do the work. Saint John Hotel Villas & Spa is in Agios Ioannis, one of the island's celebrated sunset spots.
Hotels with a private chapel.** Kivotos and Ftelia Bay Hotel each have a private chapel on their grounds, and Saint John offers vows at Agia Fotini Chapel.
Hotels with a private chapel.** Kivotos and Ftelia Bay Hotel each have a private chapel on their grounds, and Saint John offers vows at Agia Fotini Chapel.
Hotels with a private chapel.** Kivotos and Ftelia Bay Hotel each have a private chapel on their grounds, and Saint John offers vows at Agia Fotini Chapel.
Beachfront resorts.** These give you the ceremony, the dinner and the guest rooms under one events team. Mykonos Blu describes itself as a Cycladic settlement on the waterfront, with 103 guest rooms.

Large resorts with several spaces.** For a long guest list, a resort with more than one terrace lets the welcome drinks, the ceremony and the dinner each have their own setting. Saint John lists several ceremony and reception spaces, all with sea views.
Mykonos Blu, Psarou.** A five-star beachfront hotel with dedicated wedding specialists, customised menus and vow renewals as well as weddings.
Mykonos Blu, Psarou.** A five-star beachfront hotel with dedicated wedding specialists, customised menus and vow renewals as well as weddings.
Ceremonies take place on The Ocean Balcony, just above Psarou beach, for up to 60 guests, and the wedding party can then move to the L'Archipel restaurant and pool area for up to 120.
Kivotos.** A beachfront boutique hotel with a private chapel on its grounds, suited to an intimate wedding.
Its most popular reception setting is the area around the main pool on the lower level, facing the Aegean.
The hotel offers three named wedding packages, and its own wedding coordinators help with items including municipal paperwork and the marriage licence.
Saint John Hotel Villas & Spa, Agios Ioannis.** Vows can be held at Agia Fotini Chapel, on the sunset balcony or on the deck, with receptions in spaces including Theatraki, Ilios and Thalatta.
The hotel describes its weddings as running from intimate gatherings to large weddings with up to 800 guests, from welcome cocktails to five-course gala dinners.
Ftelia Bay Hotel, Ftelia Beach.** A boutique hotel where the ceremony and pre-dinner cocktails can be held at its private chapel, with traditional architecture and sea views.
The open-air pool area can host the celebration, and guests can stay in the hotel's rooms and suites.

Royal Myconian, Elia Beach.** Part of the Myconian Collection, whose events team hosts weddings across its venues, with a pool terrace and a private spot on Elia Beach.

A few patterns matter for a wedding. From June to August, rain all but disappears at Naxos, with under one rain day a month in July and August.
October is different: rain rises to 38.6 mm across 5.5 days, and April sees 6.0 rain days.
May and September sit between, with mean maximums of 22.1°C and 25.1°C.

The wind deserves as much attention as the temperature. At Naxos the prevailing wind blows from the north in every month, and the station's mean wind readings run higher from July to October than in May and June.
On an island known as the island of the winds, ask every venue where the ceremony sits relative to that north wind, and what shelter it has.
As at November 2026, [Smartraveller's advice for Greece](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/europe/greece) is to exercise normal safety precautions.
Heat.** Heatwaves are frequent in Greece over the summer months and can cause heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
Plan water, hats, light fabrics, shade and air-conditioned rest for guests, and set a summer ceremony later in the day.
Wildfire.** Wildfires occur during the extended summer period, from June to September, including near tourist areas, and can start with little warning and travel quickly.
Wind and ferries.** Ferry services can be delayed or cancelled in bad weather, mainly because of strong winds.
Guests arriving by sea should check the forecast and reconfirm departures with their travel provider.
Swimming.** Boat traffic, coastal hazards, strong currents and marine life all call for care, and sea conditions can change quickly.
Most drownings happen on beaches without a lifeguard or outside lifeguard hours, so point guests to patrolled beaches.
The ground itself.** Greece is in an active seismic zone and experiences earthquakes and volcanic activity.
Crowds.** The tourist season runs from May to October, with high temperatures and large crowds at popular seaports.

Many countries ask you to prove you are not already married, and each decides what proof it accepts.
The most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages.
Those registry certificates can be a statement of no record of a previous marriage, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate.
Local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, a late spouse's death certificate, and your original birth certificate and passport.
Regional and national laws can differ, so contact the destination's embassy or consulate for the specifics.

At the embassy in Athens.** The [Australian Embassy in Athens](https://greece.embassy.gov.au/athn/notarial.html) witnesses CNI applications, issues CNIs and witnesses notices of intended marriage.
All notarial services need an appointment, Monday to Friday, 9am to 12.30pm, though CNI and apostille documents can be sent by post.
They are ready for collection within two working days unless same-day collection is arranged in advance, or can be returned by mail, and a fee applies.
The embassy gives no legal advice, and you are responsible for knowing which service you need.
It does not witness signatures on overseas documents, and honorary consuls are not authorised to provide notarial services.
Legalising your documents.** Ask the Greek authority which documents it needs and which must be legalised, and whether that means an apostille or an authentication certificate.
Documents that are not original Australian public documents must first be notarised by an Australian Notary Public.
The apostille or authentication certificate is applied directly to the document.
If you do not want your originals marked, have a notarised copy legalised instead, and check the Greek authority accepts it.

Requests go on the Document Legalisation Request Form, signed in front of an authorised witness, and can be lodged by appointment at an Australian Passport Office, at many Australian embassies and consulates overseas, or by registered mail to the Authentications Section in Melbourne or Sydney; a fee applies.
Processing times vary, with delays at the end of the school year, in peak holiday periods and for incomplete requests.
An Australian-issued apostille can be verified online.

You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law had it happened here.
Australia does not recognise an overseas marriage where either person is already married, is not old enough to marry, is too closely related to the other, or was forced to marry.
A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but it may not work as proof of a name change.
If either of you plans to change your name, check with your state registry of births, deaths and marriages before you fly, and talk to a lawyer to confirm the certificate is valid in Australia.

Entry.** Greece is in the Schengen area, and Australians can make short trips without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period.
On arrival, Australian passport holders register fingerprints and a photo under the European Entry/Exit System, which is free and needs no action beforehand but may slow the border.
